column5: house, servants, ox, donkey, every possession
column6: The anti-coveting command gathers a neighbor's house, male and female servants, ox, donkey, and other possessions into one household inventory, closely matching the commentary's owner-house-animal-slave tableau.

column5: servant chooses master, wife, children, household
column6: The Hebrew servant says that he loves his master, wife, and children and will not go free; this gives a legal counter-case in which continued belonging is explicitly voiced as a choice.

column5: doorpost, pierced ear, permanent service
column6: The master brings the willing servant to the doorpost and pierces his ear for lifelong service, a concrete ritualization of ownership and enduring service in the master's house.

column5: Sabbath rest for ox, donkey, servant
column6: The Sabbath command joins the ox and donkey to the child of the slave woman and resident alien in receiving rest, placing a divine limit on the labor imposed upon both working animals and dependent people.

column5: servant rests “as you do”
column6: The Decalogue's Sabbath law requires the male and female servant to rest as the owner rests; it turns the master-slave relation into an equality of rest before God.

column5: Israel released from serving Egypt
column6: When Israel has gone, Egypt describes the loss as letting them go “from serving us”; the phrasing gives the Pharaoh-Israel bondage in the commentary a direct narrative counterpart.

column5: human master bounded by sin against God
column6: Joseph says his master has withheld nothing but his wife, yet refuses because the act would be a sin against God; the human householder's wide control is subordinated to a higher Lord.

column5: direct “I am your servant”; bonds loosed
column6: The psalmist directly calls himself God's servant and son of God's maidservant, then says God has loosed his bonds; it keeps divine servanthood and liberation together in one prayer.

column5: bow, kneel, maker
column6: The congregation is summoned to bow down and kneel before YHWH its maker, a close liturgical image of embodied abasement before the creator.

column5: people of pasture, flock of God's hand
column6: The worshippers are God's people and the flock of his hand; it combines animal dependence, the owner's hand, and collective divine belonging.

column5: life of animals and humans in God's hand
column6: Job places the life of every living creature and the breath of all humanity in God's hand, extending the commentary's hand-held possession figure beyond livestock to all life.

column5: everything under heaven belongs to God
column6: God asks who could give first so that God owed repayment, because all under heaven is God's; it joins universal possession to divine non-dependence.

column5: earth and inhabitants belong to YHWH
column6: The psalm's opening ownership formula gives YHWH the earth, its fullness, the world, and its inhabitants, an explicit scriptural horizon for “Lord of the worlds.”

column5: all comes from God; gifts returned
column6: David's praise says all things come from God and that Israel gives only what is already God's; it makes praise an acknowledgment that human possessions remain received goods.

column5: wise servant shares a son's inheritance
column6: A prudent servant rules over a shameful son and shares the inheritance with the brothers, overturning a fixed hierarchy of owner, household, and slave.

column5: one guarding a master is honored
column6: Proverbs says the one who keeps or attends to a master will be honored, a compact wisdom parallel to the commentary's secondary possibility that service and honor meet.

column5: exalted servant
column6: God's servant is described as raised, lifted up, and greatly exalted, supplying a scriptural servant-and-honor trajectory beside the commentary's muʿabbad sense.

column5: fasting that breaks every yoke
column6: The fast God chooses loosens bonds, frees the oppressed, and breaks every yoke; it makes worship answer human subjugation by liberation rather than by extending it.

column5: Father, potter, clay, work of hands
column6: The prayer calls God Father and potter and the people clay made by God's hand, a creation-and-forming image for dependence that does not reduce them to household property.

column5: clay in potter's hand, house of Israel
column6: God compares the house of Israel to clay in a potter's hand, a particularly close biblical image for formed material held under a maker's authority.

column5: refusal to serve gods or worship the image
column6: The Judean servants tell the king that they will neither serve his gods nor worship his golden image, a concrete refusal of a ruler's imposed cultic mastery.

column5: judge, lawgiver, king
column6: YHWH is named Israel's judge, lawgiver, and king; the verse gathers the judicial and sovereign dimensions that meet in the commentary's Mālik of the Day of dīn.

column5: God brings every deed into judgment
column6: The closing maxim says God will bring every deed, hidden or open, into judgment, providing an explicit Hebrew Bible counterpart to the reckoning implied by Day of dīn.

column5: humble king riding a donkey
column6: Zion's king comes righteous and victorious yet humble, mounted on a donkey; the royal figure unites authority, lowliness, and a domesticated animal in a configuration that reverses the commentary's unlowered master.

column5: make straight paths for feet
column6: Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so that the lame may be healed rather than put out of joint, turning the made-level road into a communal moral action.

column5: gentle king mounted on donkey
column6: Matthew presents the king as gentle and mounted on a donkey, carrying Zechariah's master-humility-and-domesticated-animal figure into the Gospel entry scene.

column5: servant falls before master over debt
column6: The servant falls down before his master and begs for patience over the debt, giving a literal scene of servile prostration, ownership, and reckoning.

column5: master releases servant and forgives debt
column6: The master is moved with compassion, releases the servant, and cancels the debt; this masterly authority is expressed through liberation rather than permanent subjection.

column5: direct prayer to creator as Sovereign Master
column6: The community addresses God as despota, the Sovereign Master who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; it joins direct address, mastery, and creation in one prayer.

column5: Cornelius falls at a human's feet
column6: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet and prostrates before him, staging the very transfer of honor to a human figure that the commentary's limit on human lords excludes.

column5: Peter refuses human prostration
column6: Peter raises Cornelius and says that he too is human, turning the preceding act into an explicit rejection of worshipful elevation of a person.

column5: bodies offered as living sacrifice and worship
column6: Paul calls the presentation of embodied life to God a living sacrifice and rational worship, giving worship a concrete, whole-person form beyond a merely verbal confession.

column5: slaves serve the Lord Christ
column6: In an instruction to household slaves, Paul says that the service ultimately rendered is to the Lord Christ and promises an inheritance, placing earthly service under a different master and reward.

column5: free people as slaves of God
column6: Believers are to live as free people while also as God's slaves; the deliberate pairing gives a Christian reversal of the commentary's ordinary contrast between freedom and owned status.

column5: acceptable worship with reverence and awe
column6: The community is to offer acceptable worship to God with reverence and awe because it receives an unshakable kingdom, a liturgical form of humble service before sovereignty.

column5: all appear before Christ's judgment seat
column6: All people must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive according to their deeds, an individual accounting scene for the Day of dīn dimension.

column5: a fixed day for judging the world
column6: Paul says God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, making the day-and-judgment element explicit in the same speech that calls God creator and Lord.

column5: only Sovereign, King of kings, Lord of lords
column6: The doxology calls God the only Sovereign and the King of kings and Lord of lords, a compact New Testament royal-master formulation beside Mālik.

column5: direct praise to the creator
column6: The heavenly elders say directly, “You are worthy,” because God created all things by his will; it closely joins praise, direct address, and creation-based sovereignty.

column5: Sovereign Lord asked to judge
column6: The martyrs address God as Sovereign Lord and ask when God will judge, bringing master-language and the delayed final judgment into a single direct prayer.

column5: acquiring a Hebrew servant acquires a master
column6: The Talmud's maxim that one who acquires a Hebrew servant acquires a master develops Torah's service law into a reversal: the owner must meet the servant's needs so fully that mastery is ethically displaced.

column5: slaves serve for God's glory and better freedom
column6: Ignatius tells enslaved Christians to serve more diligently for God's glory so that they may receive a better freedom from God, preserving the tension between social servitude and divine freedom.
